blocks.title: Electrophilic addition
blocks.text: A reaction in which an electrophile is added to the double bond of an alkene is an electrophilic addition reaction.

The C=C of an alkene is a region of high electron density and so is susceptible to attack by electrophiles. An alkene reacts with an electrophile to give a carbocation intermediate, which then reacts with a nucleophile; in the generalised mechanism of Figure 11.13, X+ is the electrophile and Y- the nucleophile. Only the mechanisms of halogen addition and hydrogen halide addition are studied here.

blocks.alt: Step 1: a curly arrow from the C=C double bond of an alkene to an electrophile X+ forms a carbocation with X on one carbon and the positive charge on the other. Step 2: a nucleophile Y- attacks the positive carbon, giving the addition product with X and Y on neighbouring carbons.
blocks.caption: Generalized mechanism of electrophilic addition (original diagram after Figure 11.13).

blocks.text: 1. Halogenation

Halogenation is the addition of chlorine or bromine. When bromine water (red-brown) is added to ethene in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride its colour is discharged at once; the reaction is used to identify unsaturation: CH2=CH2 + Br2 gives BrCH2-CH2Br. Mechanism: (i) Br2 is non-polar, but as it approaches the double bond the high electron density repels the Br-Br electron pair away from the nearer bromine, which becomes slightly positive (an induced dipole) and acts as the electrophile; (ii) the pi electrons attack the positive bromine, which accepts a pair of electrons from the C=C, giving a highly reactive carbocation intermediate; (iii) the carbocation reacts with Br- (nucleophile) to give 1,2-dibromoethane (Figure 11.14).

blocks.alt: Ethene approaches Br2, which becomes polarised (d+ and d-). A curly arrow from the C=C bond to the d+ bromine and another from the Br-Br bond to the far bromine give a carbocation with Br on one carbon and a bromide ion. The bromide ion attacks the positive carbon to give 1,2-dibromoethane, BrCH2-CH2Br; bromine water is decolourised, a test for C=C.
blocks.caption: Electrophilic addition mechanism of ethene and Br2 (original diagram after Figure 11.14).

blocks.alt: An H-Br molecule with H marked d+ and Br marked d-, and a dipole arrow from H to Br. Labels say bromine is more electronegative and pulls the bonding electrons, so the electron-deficient hydrogen is the electrophile.
blocks.caption: Polarity of the HBr molecule (original diagram after Figure 11.15).

blocks.alt: Step 1: ethene's pi bond attacks the d+ hydrogen of HBr while the H-Br electrons move to bromine, giving the carbocation CH3-CH2+ and a bromide ion. Step 2: the bromide ion adds to the positive carbon to give bromoethane, CH3-CH2-Br.
blocks.caption: Electrophilic addition mechanism of HBr to ethene (original diagram after Figure 11.16).

blocks.text: 2. Hydrohalogenation

An alkene reacts with dry gaseous hydrogen halide at room temperature to give a halogenoalkane: CH2=CH2 + HBr gives CH3CH2Br, bromoethane. Hydrogen halides are among the simplest polar substances with permanent dipoles that add to alkenes (Figure 11.15); all of HBr, HCl, HI and HF add across C=C the same way, the rate increasing from HF to HI. The product depends on whether the alkene is symmetrical or unsymmetrical.

Addition to symmetrical alkenes: with ethene only one product is possible. The nucleophilic pi bond attacks the hydrogen of the hydrogen halide, hydrogen bromide gives a bromide ion, and ethene becomes a carbocation by adding hydrogen to one of the double-bonded carbons; the bromide ion (nucleophile) then attacks the carbocation to give bromoethane (Figure 11.16).

Addition to unsymmetrical alkenes: two products are theoretically possible. HBr with propene could give 2-bromopropane or 1-bromopropane; experimentally the major product is 2-bromopropane and the minor 1-bromopropane. Markovnikov's rule applies: when a polar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part of the reagent attaches to the double-bonded carbon bearing the smaller number of hydrogens. Mechanism (Figure 11.17): (i) the pi electrons attack the partially positive end of H-Br, which breaks heterolytically to a bromide ion; hydrogen adds to the double-bonded carbon with more hydrogens, creating a secondary (2 degree) carbocation; (ii) the bromide ion attacks the secondary carbocation to give the major product, while the minor product comes from attack on the primary carbocation.

blocks.alt: Propene, CH3-CH=CH2, with HBr follows two paths. Upper path: H adds to the end carbon, giving the more stable secondary carbocation, which takes Br- to give 2-bromopropane, the major product. Lower path: H adds to the middle carbon, giving a less stable primary carbocation and 1-bromopropane, the minor product. A note gives Markovnikov's rule.
blocks.caption: Electrophilic addition mechanism of HBr to propene (major and minor products) (original diagram after Figure 11.17).

blocks.text: 3. Hydrogenation

Hydrogenation is the addition of molecular hydrogen to an alkene in the presence of a catalyst (Ni or Pt) at 250 to 300 degrees C to give a saturated compound: CH2=CH2 + H2 over Ni gives CH3CH3. Industrially the reaction converts vegetable oil into margarine (banaspati ghee).
4. Hydration

Gaseous alkenes react with steam at high temperature and pressure with concentrated acid (H2SO4) as catalyst to form alcohols: CH2=CH2 + H2O gives C2H5OH. As in hydrohalogenation, the alkene forms a carbocation intermediate, which is then attacked by OH-.
5. Halohydration
An alkene reacts with a halogen (bromine or chlorine) in the presence of water to form a halohydrin; ethene gives a bromohydrin or chlorohydrin: CH2=CH2 + Br2 + H2O gives BrCH2-CH2OH, 2-bromoethanol.
6. Epoxidation

Epoxidation of alkenes gives an oxygen-containing three-membered cyclic ether, an epoxide. Ethene can be converted to ethylene oxide with various oxidising agents, or with molecular oxygen and a transition metal catalyst (Ag), which forms the epoxide directly from the alkene. Epoxides are converted into diols by acid hydrolysis: ethylene oxide with H+/H2O gives ethane-1,2-diol.
7. Ozonolysis

Ozonolysis is the oxidative cleaving of alkenes with ozone, O3, a reactive allotrope of oxygen; it is used to identify the structure of unknown alkenes by breaking them into smaller, more easily identified pieces. Alkenes react with ozone to form ozonides, which are reduced (Zn/H2O) to carbonyl compounds (aldehydes or ketones), and these can be reduced further to alcohols: C2H4 + O3 gives C2H4O3, which gives 2 CH2O (methanal). Propene gives ethanal and methanal, reducible to ethanol and methanol.
8. Polymerisation

Polymerisation is the formation of extremely long molecules (polymers) from small reactive molecules (monomers) that join together. Addition polymerisation, in which many monomers each containing at least one C=C form long polymer chains as the only product, is one of the most important addition reactions of alkenes and the basis of the plastics industry. As in other additions, the pi bond of each C=C breaks and the monomers link through new C-C single bonds; a polymer is a long-chain molecule of many repeating units. Ethene gives poly(ethene), chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene), PVC. The repeating unit is the smallest group of atoms that, connected one after another, makes up the chain, shown in square brackets; in poly(alkenes) and substituted poly(alkenes) made from one monomer it is the monomer with the C=C changed to C-C.

blocks.alt: Top left: a table of eight reactions of ethene with reagents, conditions and products. Top right: buta-1,3-diene with a dashed red arc showing delocalised p orbitals. Middle right: the five kinds of structural isomerism and stereoisomerism. Bottom left: organic oxidation and reduction equations. Bottom: the addition polymerisation of ethene and chloroethene with the repeating unit.
blocks.caption: Reactions of ethene, conjugated dienes, isomerism and organic redox (original diagram after topics 11.8.1, 11.9, 11.10.1 and 11.11).
blocks.long_description: Starting from ethene, hydrogen over nickel gives ethane, hydrogen bromide gives bromoethane, bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethane and is decolourised, steam with acid gives ethanol, bromine in water gives bromoethanol, oxygen over silver gives the epoxide that hydrolyses to ethane-1,2-diol, ozone followed by zinc and water cuts the double bond to two molecules of methanal, and many molecules join head to tail into poly(ethene). A diene whose double bonds alternate with a single bond spreads its pi electrons over all four carbons, which stabilises it and lets butadiene polymerise to rubber. Isomers share a formula but differ in chain, position of a group, functional group, distribution about a functional group, or a shifted proton, while stereoisomers differ only in space. Adding oxygen or removing hydrogen is organic oxidation and the reverse is reduction.
